Why Founders Cannot Sleep and What Lack of Sleep Does to Their Work
Why founders find it hard to stop thinking about work at night, and three changes that help.
Why Founders Cannot Sleep and What Lack of Sleep Does to Their Work

It is 1:40am. The house is quiet, the laptop is closed, and your mind is still going over a board meeting that will not happen for another six days. If you have wondered why founders cannot sleep even when they are exhausted, the answer is not a lack of discipline. It is biology. The habits that help you build a company, such as staying alert to problems and refusing to leave them unresolved, also make it hard to stop thinking about the company at night.

This article looks at what happens in a founder mind at night, what regularly sleeping only six hours a night does to the skills you rely on most, and three changes that are supported by research and that fit around a demanding schedule.
Why founders cannot sleep: a mind that stays alert
Falling asleep requires your nervous system to move from being alert to feeling safe. Founders spend their days doing the opposite. They train themselves to stay alert to problems all day.
Cortisol arrives at the wrong time

Cortisol follows a daily pattern. It should reach its highest level in the first hour after waking, which is what gets you out of bed, and fall steadily until it reaches its lowest level around midnight. Long periods of pressure change that pattern and delay it. Reading email late at night, an investor call at 9pm, or a cash flow problem you are still thinking about at 11pm keeps cortisol high at the time it should be falling. The result is a body that is tired and a mind that is alert.
Decision fatigue does not mean a quiet mind

A founder can make hundreds of decisions in a day. Most of them are small and many of them are unresolved. You might expect that load to leave you tired enough to sleep. In practice, your mind keeps returning to unfinished decisions. It goes over the options and the possible results because the decisions have not been settled.
The rumination loop

Rumination is the habit of thinking about a problem again and again without solving it. It is closely linked to taking longer to fall asleep and to waking during the night. For founders the subject is rarely abstract. It is a hire that is not working, a customer who left, or the number of months of money the company has left. Lying awake creates frustration, frustration makes you more alert, and being more alert pushes sleep further away.
Research from UC San Francisco found that 49 percent of entrepreneurs reported at least one lifetime mental health condition, a rate well above comparison groups.

None of this means something is wrong with you. It means the traits that help build companies, such as staying alert, continuing when things are hard, and refusing to leave problems alone, need a deliberate way to stop at night.
What six hours a night actually does
Plenty of founders run on six hours and feel fine. The research suggests "fine" is the problem.

In a landmark study at the University of Pennsylvania, Van Dongen and colleagues restricted healthy adults to six hours in bed per night for two weeks. By the end, their attention and working memory had declined to a level comparable with people kept awake for up to two full nights. The striking part was not the decline. It was that the six-hour group rated themselves as only slightly sleepy. Their performance kept falling while their sense of how they were doing levelled off.
After two weeks of six-hour nights, cognitive performance fell to levels seen after up to two nights without any sleep, while participants felt only slightly tired.

For a founder, the abilities that suffer are the thinking skills you use to run the company. They include setting priorities, holding several tasks in mind at once, stopping yourself from sending an impulsive reply, and moving between deep work and frequent interruptions. These skills are among the first to suffer when you do not sleep enough.

Lack of sleep also changes how you look. A study published in the BMJ asked observers to rate photographs of the same people after a normal night of sleep and after sleep deprivation. The faces of the sleep deprived people were judged less healthy, more tired, and less attractive. Other people notice the change before you do.
Three changes supported by research for busy schedules

The standard advice, such as no screens, a warm bath, and lavender, was not written for someone answering messages from people in three time zones. These three changes address the specific causes described above and can fit into a real schedule.
1. Write down your unfinished tasks before bed

A study at Baylor University compared two groups before bed. One spent five minutes writing about tasks they had completed. The other spent five minutes writing a specific to-do list for the coming days. The to-do group fell asleep faster, and the more specific their list, the faster they slept.

Writing a task down helps because your mind no longer needs to keep reminding you about it. Keep a notebook by the bed, not a phone. Before you turn the lights out, write the three things you will deal with tomorrow and the first action for each one.
2. Return your cortisol to its normal daily pattern

You cannot force cortisol down at 11pm, but you can shape the pattern that leads there. Get outdoor light within an hour of waking, even ten minutes on a cloudy day, to support the normal morning rise in cortisol. Do your hardest thinking and hold your most difficult meetings before mid afternoon. Stop high stakes conversations two hours before bed, and treat late investor or legal calls as exceptions, not the normal routine.
Caffeine belongs here too. In one sleep lab study, caffeine taken six hours before bed still cut total sleep by more than an hour. A flat white at 3pm still affects your sleep that night.
3. Protect a fixed wake time, not a fixed bedtime

Founders rarely control when the day ends. They can usually control when it starts. A consistent wake time, including weekends within about an hour, stabilises your body clock faster than any bedtime rule. Work out your bedtime from your wake time. If you need to be up at 6:30, aim to be in bed by 11:00, and treat that sleep time as fixed in your schedule.

If you wake at 3am and cannot fall asleep again within twenty minutes, get up, keep the lights low, and read something dull until you feel sleepy. Lying in bed awake and worrying makes you more likely to associate being in bed with worrying about problems.
Measure it before you try to fix it

Sleep costs nothing, and it is hard to judge from the inside, because tiredness changes how tired you think you are. Founders who improve their sleep are usually the ones who track it, not the ones who rely on how they feel.
